history.title: Crew Launch Week 11: Your Part of the Whole

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Perseverance. "I persevere to produce high quality work."

This week is about high quality work when the work belongs to a group: naming your part, finishing it, and asking early when it depends on someone else.

1. Read **Your Part of the Whole** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **What, Where, By When** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Named Part or Hope?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is about Lena and Omar's notebook.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Teamwork Builder](#sel-hub/teamwork?station=sel_station_crew_launch_teamwork). Look at Roles, then write a Communication Plan for a real group you are in this trimester. Then open [DEAR MAN](#sel-hub/dearMan?station=sel_station_crew_launch_teamwork) and build the ask you would send a teammate whose part you are waiting on.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your part of the whole for one real group.
8. Lock it in with **Remember What, Where, By When**.
9. Finish with the **Propose Challenge: A Parts List for Our Group**.

Your commitment: this week, in one real group task, say your part of the whole out loud (what, where, by when) and finish it before the deadline. 🧩

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Your Part of the Whole
history.data:
## Your Part of the Whole

**HOWL: "I persevere to produce high quality work."**

At King, a lot of the work that matters is group work. **Expeditions** end in a product a team made together: a field guide, a documentary, a museum exhibit. High **quality** work, the Perseverance **HOWL**, is easy to picture when it is yours alone. When it belongs to four people, it gets complicated fast. Who did what? Who did nothing? Who did everything at midnight the night before and resents the other three?

Here is the trap most groups fall into. The work is assigned to the group, so nobody in the group owns any particular piece of it. Everyone assumes someone else has the graphs. The graphs do not exist until Thursday night, when one person makes them badly because there is no time to make them well. The product is worse than any one member could have made alone, and everyone is a little angry. Researchers call one cause of this **social loafing**: people put in less effort when responsibility is spread across a group. It is not laziness. It is what happens when a **part** has no name on it.

The fix is a sentence. "My part of the **whole** is the two data graphs, on the shared slide, by Wednesday." What, where, and by when. Once every part has a sentence like that, the group has a plan instead of a **hope**. Once every sentence has a name, the loafing mostly stops, because it is **visible**.

Here is a moment from a fictional **Crew**. Lena's expedition group has a poster due Friday. On Monday she says her sentence out loud: the two graphs, on the slide, by Wednesday. On Tuesday she realizes the data she needs is in Omar's notebook and Omar is out sick. She could wait. Instead she uses what she learned in week 5 and asks: a text to Omar, "Could you send a photo of the water-test page?" The photo comes. The graphs are done Wednesday. On Friday the poster is good, and the group knows exactly whose graphs those are.

Persevering in a group has two halves. The first is finishing your part, on time, at the quality you would want if your name were the only one on it. The second is **asking early** when your part **depends** on someone else's, instead of waiting and then blaming. Both halves are yours. Neither one requires the rest of the group to be perfect.

One more thing. Sometimes your part is done and someone else's is not, and Friday is coming. You are allowed to help. You are also allowed to say, calmly, to the group and to the teacher, which part was yours. That is not tattling. That is what "my part of the whole" means: the whole is shared, and the parts have names.

questions.question: What does the reading say is the trap most groups fall into?

The work belongs to the group, so no piece belongs to anyone

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if my group will not agree on parts?
data.answer: Then name yours anyway, out loud and in the shared file. "I am doing the graphs, on the slide, by Wednesday." One named part often makes the others visible. If the group still will not, that is a sentence for the teacher on Tuesday, not Friday.

data.question: What if I end up doing everything?
data.answer: You are allowed to help. You are also allowed to say, calmly, which parts were yours. Write it down as it happens; a parts list with names is fair to everyone, including you.

data.question: Is asking a teammate for their part nagging?
data.answer: Asking early, once, with a date, is planning. Asking on Thursday night, three times, in capitals, is what happens when nobody asked early.

data.question: What if my part depends on someone who never delivers?
data.answer: Ask early with a date. If the date passes, tell the teacher that day, with your part done and the dependency named. That is the whole job; the rest is not yours to carry.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Perseverance HOWL says you persevere to produce high quality work. In a group, that means your part finished at your own quality and your asks made early. Your teachers score HOWLs; Crew is where you practice them.

cards.aiExample: W-W-W: What, Where, When. Three W's, like a web address for your part. If the sentence is missing a W, the part is a hope.

history.title: Propose Challenge: A Parts List for Our Group

data.title: A Parts List for Our Group
data.instructions: For one real group task this trimester, propose a parts list to your group: every part with what, where, by when, and a name, plus the asks each part depends on. Get the group to agree, use it, and report what happened by Friday.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behavior is persevering to produce high quality work. A parts list the student proposes and the group adopts makes every part visible, which is what stops loafing and what makes a finished, named part possible.

brief.context: You are in a real group with a real product due. Right now the plan is probably a hope. You are going to propose a parts list and see whether the group will use it.
brief.role: A group member proposing a plan
brief.audience: Your group, and the teacher who assigned the product
brief.drivingQuestion: Can a parts list with names, places, and dates turn our hope into a plan, and does the product get better?
brief.seedDirection: List every piece of the product. Put one name on each. Add where it lives and when it is due, earlier than the final deadline. Mark which parts depend on which. Propose it to the group and revise it with them. Use it for the week.
lockedLessonFacts: When the work belongs to the group, no piece belongs to anyone, and it gets made badly at the last minute.
A part is named by what, where, and by when.
Persevering in a group means finishing your part and asking early when it depends on someone.
You may help, and you may say which part was yours.
openQuestions: Where will the list live so everyone can see it?
What happens if a date passes?
stakeholders: The member whose part everyone else depends on
The audience the product is for
criteria: Every part has what, where, by when, and a name
Dependencies are marked with an ask and a date
The group agreed to the list, with at least one change from them
The Friday report says which parts landed on time
Uses at least three glossary words
constraints: The list lives in a shared place
Part deadlines are before the final deadline
Your own part is finished at your own quality
brief.deliverable: The agreed parts list (with names, places, dates, and asks) and a half-page Friday report: what landed, what did not, and what you would change.

parallelExample.context: A fictional group had a museum-exhibit panel due Friday and no plan.
parallelExample.move: One member proposed: research, on the shared doc, Tuesday (Kai); layout, in the design file, Thursday (Mei, depends on Kai); captions, in the file, Wednesday (Dev). Mei asked Kai on Monday for the research by Tuesday. Three of three landed.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows that the ask sits inside the list, dated, so nobody has to nag on Thursday.

supports.frameStarter: Our whole is ____, due ____. Parts: ____ (____, by ____). ____ depends on ____, so the ask is ____ by ____.
frameChoices: The group changed ____ in my list.
On Friday, ____ of ____ parts landed on time.
coachPrompts: Whose part is first in the chain, and does that person know?
Is your own part named as tightly as everyone else's?

data.coachHint: If a group refuses the list, the student still names their own part and reports that. A proposal the group declined is still a proposal made.
data.sourceExcerpt: The fix is a sentence. What, where, and by when. Once every part has a sentence like that, the group has a plan instead of a hope. Once every sentence has a name, the loafing mostly stops, because it is visible.
